Thirty years of political violence in Northern Ireland, from about 1968 to the Good Friday Agreement of 1998. More than 3,500 people died.

Northern Ireland was made in 1921 when Ireland was divided, with a Protestant majority that wanted to stay British (unionists) and a Catholic minority, many of whom wanted a united Ireland (nationalists). Catholics faced bias in housing and jobs, and in Derry the voting districts were drawn to keep unionists in control. A civil rights movement began marching in 1968 and met police batons and loyalist attacks.

The riots of August 1969 brought in the British Army. The Provisional IRA split off and began a campaign to force a British withdrawal. Loyalist groups answered with killings of their own. Bloody Sunday in 1972 pushed many young Catholics toward the IRA. Other turning points were Bloody Friday, the murder of Lord Mountbatten and the 1981 hunger strike.

Ceasefires in 1994 and talks led to the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, which set up shared government.
sum: Thirty years of political violence in Northern Ireland, from about 1968 to the Good Friday Agreement of 1998. More than 3,500 people died.
